newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK --Housing, industrial production.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK --Housing, industrial production.

text.p: A U.S. Treasury market bouyed by a benign consumer price report faces two challenges on Wednesday -- the government's March housing starts report and Federal Reserve figures on March industrial production.

A wave of relief and technically inspired buying lifted the U.S. Treasury market on Tuesday after the Labor Department reported a more subdued March Consumer Price Index (CPI) than economists and investors had anticipated.
In late trade on Tuesday, the 30-year Treasury bond had risen 31/32 to 94-9/32 to yield 7.09 percent.
But analysts said the market's attention would soon have to return to a strong real economy.
On Wednesday, the March housing starts report and the March industrial production/capacity utilization figures could compel bond investors to look that reality squarely in the eye, economists said.

In a Reuters poll, economists estimated that housing starts fell 4.45 percent to an annualized rate of 1.46 million in March from February's annualized rate of 1.528 million units, the fastest pace in nearly three years.
Experts said February's exceptional gains were related to the weather and that even with the expected pull back in March, the market for new homes remained robust.

Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets, said a March housing starts number of 1.50 or higher would deal the market a setback. On the other hand, for bond prices to get any upward mileage out of the housing starts figures, starts would have to come in near 1.40 million or less, he said.
After the 0830 EDT/1230 GMT housing report come industrial production and capacity use figures at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT.

Data on manufacturing payroll growth and on the average manufacturing workweek length offered by the March U.S. employment report point to a healthy industrial production gain for March, economists said.
In a Reuters poll, economists, on average, forecasted a 0.6 percent rise in March industrial production after a 0.5 percent production gain in February.
A 0.5 percent, 0.6 percent, 0.7 percent or 0.8 percent industrial production gain would be neutral for the market, said Karydakis.

But economists added that such back-to-back production gains would show that the economy is still strong and could do nothing to diminish expectations that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates again this spring or summer.
The Fed raised short-term interest rates in March for the first time in more than two years, boosting its Federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5-1/2 percent.
Elliott Platt said the housing and industrial production data that the market gets on Wednesday could leave it little changed from Tuesday's closing levels.
The benign March CPI took a lot of bearishness out of the market, Platt said, providing some protective armor against data like those expected on Wednesday.
"The CPI is indicating that there is still no flow-through of inflationary pressures into actual inflation," Platt said. "That's going to give the market a real base of support."

Platt said he doubted the 30-year bond yield would climb higher than 7.125 percent before the trio of economic data due at the end of April and at the start of May -- the quarterly Employment Cost Index (ECI), the April National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM), and April U.S. payrolls data.
"After this CPI, it will be hard for the market to deteriorate just because a couple of March economic numbers look strong," he said.
Dealers said Fed funds will likely open between 5-1/2 percent and 5-9/16 percent on Wednesday.
(( -- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679))
